title: Slowly Changing Dimensions Overview
description: Notes for Slowly Changing Dimensions Overview

content.text: Data Warehouses and Analytics - Study Notes

Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCDs) are a core technique in data warehousing that enables the preservation of historical integrity in analytical systems. Unlike operational databases that overwrite past information, data warehouses use SCDs to meticulously track every change to descriptive attributes within dimension tables (e.g., Customer, Product). This allows analytical queries to reflect past states accurately, enabling trend analysis, performance measurement, and strategic decision-making based on complete history.

A new column is added to store the previous value of an attribute, preserving partial history (current and one previous state).

Type 1 and Type 2 are the most commonly used. SCDs are fundamental for preserving historical data in data warehouses, ensuring accurate time-based analysis. Choosing the appropriate type (e.g., Type 2 for full history, Type 6 for combined row/column tracking) is crucial for meeting specific analytical requirements. Proper implementation ensures data integrity, supports complex business intelligence, and facilitates informed decision-making over time.

In a star schema, every foreign key in a fact table must join to its associated dimension. However, new fact data may arrive before the corresponding dimension records are available (late-arriving dimensions), causing join failures. This can happen due to:
Facts may arrive in close proximity to dimension updates, but not exactly synchronized.
Entity migration triggers SCD changes; facts streamed afterward use updated dimensions that haven't arrived yet.
If ETL jobs are not properly ordered, dimensions may be processed after facts.
Put fact records into "suspense" (process now and hydrate later).
Detect early-arriving facts and retry (reconciliation pattern).
Solution 1: Process Now and Hydrate Later
Incoming fact data is stored in a dedicated "suspense" or "retry" table with default values in dimension columns. A separate hydration process periodically tries to update missing dimension keys.
Does not work if dimension keys are foreign keys in fact tables (data integrity constraint).
If facts are written to multiple destinations, hydration must update all of them for consistency.
Fundamentally unpredictable — no guarantee when (or if) missing dimension data will arrive.
Risk of facts cycling endlessly through retries, never becoming visible to users.
For example, in an aviation bus matrix, a
dimension might contain a "N/A" record for flights that were not delayed. Similarly, for late-arriving dimensions, create a specially-created dimension record with description "Not known yet".
For optional relationships, often there's no need for a lookup; special records are allocated meaningful (negative) surrogate keys.
When the dimension data eventually arrives, you must go back and update fact records pointing to "Not known yet" — expensive and error-prone.
For SCD2, the natural key must be stored alongside the surrogate key in the fact record to enable later updates.
For SCD1, if using a surrogate key, store the hash of the dimension PK in the fact table as a FK to facilitate later correction.
Solution 3: Early Detection and Reconciliation Pattern (Recommended)

Detect early-arriving facts (facts for which the corresponding dimension has not arrived yet), put them on hold, and retry after a period until they are processed or exhaust retries. This ensures data quality and consistency.
Reconciliation pattern using streaming data (Kafka, Spark, Delta Lake):
Transform facts and left-join to dimension tables.
If dimension missing, flag the fact record as
MERGE valid (non-retryable) records into the target delta table.
A scheduled batch job consolidates multiple failed retries for the same event into a single row in a reconciliation table, with updated retry count and status.
The streaming pipeline reads from the reconciliation table (UNION with new Kafka data) and retries the join. If still missing, write back to errors; if resolved, proceed to merge.
No need to put data back on Kafka (avoids duplicate events).
Avoids concurrent MERGE issues by using a separate reconciliation table.
Works with both streaming and batch ETLs.
Automates retries with alerting and monitoring.
Login events processed in near real-time, joined with user dimension table (updated by batch ETL).
If a user dimension is missing, the event is flagged retryable.
The reconciliation table tracks retries: e.g., event_id 29 was retried twice before successfully joining.
Monitoring: a spike in retryable records indicates a problem with the batch job loading dimensions.
Partition the reconciliation table on status column to only read unresolved records.

The reconciliation pattern is easy to plug into existing pipelines with a small boilerplate framework. It provides automated retries with built-in alerting and monitoring, ensuring data quality without manual intervention.
The fundamental difference is data layout on disk.
Values for a single row are stored contiguously. Ideal for OLTP workloads with frequent single-row reads, writes, and updates.
Values for a single column are stored contiguously. Ideal for OLAP workloads with large scans, aggregations, filtering over a subset of columns.
Row-oriented reads entire rows (even if only few columns needed); column-oriented reads only the required columns, minimizing I/O.
Column-oriented is highly effective because similar data types are stored together (low entropy). Row-oriented is less effective due to mixed types.
Column-oriented is significantly faster for analytical queries on column subsets; row-oriented faster for retrieving complete records (SELECT *).
MySQL, PostgreSQL (row); DuckDB, Snowflake, BigQuery, ClickHouse (column).

In-memory columnar format for fast analytics and cross-system data interchange. Use cases: DataFrames (Pandas, R), ML pipelines.
Open-source storage layer that adds ACID transactions, time travel, and schema enforcement on top of Parquet. (See detailed comparison below.)
Columnar systems optimized for high-speed retrieval; frequent single-row updates (OLTP) are better served by row-based databases.
Avoid wasted I/O from reading entire rows.
Because identical values are often adjacent, columnar storage compresses exceptionally well:
Replaces repeated strings with integer IDs. Best for low-cardinality columns.
Stores a value once with a count of its repetitions. Best for sorted columns or long runs of identical values.
Stores differences between consecutive values. Best for slowly changing series like timestamps.
Subtracts a minimum value and stores smaller offsets. Best for integer columns with limited range.
Tokenizes strings and builds a static dictionary of common substrings. Best for high-cardinality strings where dictionary encoding fails.
Applied on top of specialized encodings for further compression.
Reduces storage costs and speeds up queries by minimizing data read from disk.
If query needs 2 columns out of 100, reads only ~2% of total data.
Data loads into CPU registers in vectors, processed in parallel using SIMD instructions.
Process batches of thousands of values, amortizing function call overhead and leveraging CPU parallel processing.
Predicate pushdown applies WHERE filters at storage level; zone maps store min/max per block to skip irrelevant data.
Can analyze datasets larger than RAM by offloading intermediate data to disk.
Column stores organize data into immutable column chunks. Updating a row requires rewriting entire chunks. Modern systems like ClickHouse use
(lightweight deltas) to improve update performance by up to 1000×.
Historically, column stores lacked efficient joins, leading to denormalized wide tables. Modern stores have improved joins, but some denormalization still benefits query performance.
Physical organization (sort keys, partitioning) dramatically impacts performance. Sorting by commonly filtered columns (e.g., timestamp) improves compression and data skipping.
Not suitable for transactional workloads, SELECT * queries (row reconstruction overhead), small datasets, or high-concurrency single-row writes.
Delta Lake is a storage layer that builds on Parquet, adding critical features.
Advantages: column pruning, schema in metadata, better compression than row-based formats.
Pain points with multiple Parquet files:
No ACID transactions – data corruption risk.
No DML transactions or change data feed.
Slow file listing overhead in cloud storage (key-value stores).
Expensive footer reads for file skipping.
Renaming, dropping columns requires full table rewrite.

When to use Parquet instead of Delta Lake:

Interfacing with systems that don't support Delta Lake. Since Delta tables store data in Parquet files, conversion is straightforward. Delta connectors are increasingly available, so incompatibility is rare.
Conclusion: Delta Lake Wins Almost Always

For any production data system, especially in the cloud, Delta Lake provides reliability, performance, and operational simplicity that plain Parquet cannot match. It makes common operations (dropping/renaming columns, deleting rows, DML) simple and efficient. Transactions and schema enforcement prevent costly corruption. The transaction log enables fast queries via Z-Ordering and file skipping.
